text:
She was naked and, knowing my tastes,
had kept only her sounding jewels,
whose ornaments lent her the conquering air
Moorish slave women wear on festive days.

When that radiant world of gems and metal
flings its mocking sound into the air,
it plunges me into ecstasy; I madly love
things in which sound and light unite.

She lay there and allowed herself to be loved,
smiling with happiness from the high divan
upon my passion, deep and slow as the sea,
which rose toward her as toward its cliff.

Her eyes fixed upon me as upon a tamed tiger,
she dreamily tried different poses,
and candor joined to lechery
added new grace to her metamorphoses;

And her arms and legs, her thighs and flanks,
polished as oil, undulant as a swan,
passed before my lucid, tranquil eyes;
and her belly and breasts, clusters of my vine,

advanced, as warm as Angels of evil,
to trouble the peace in which my soul lay
and wrench it from the crystal rock
where it had settled, solitary and serene.

And I thought I saw united in a new design
—so greatly did her waist throw her pelvis into relief—
the hips of Antiope with the torso of a youth;
how superb the makeup upon her dark skin!

And when the lamp had resigned itself to die,
since the fire alone lit the room,
each time it breathed out a flaming flash
it flooded her amber-colored skin with blood.

translation.title: The Jewels
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The erotic gaze, art-historical allusion, and changing firelight are retained.
